name: Sara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping wire homes and repair shops under a qualified supervisor. I got a vocational certificate after the clothing workshop where I worked closed, and I'm still slower than the others at the practical tasks. I carry materials, help lay cable on the supervisor's instructions and ask for another demonstration when I need it. I don't have an electrician's licence or decide the tests and final checks myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like around the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ben does cleaning shifts, our children are grown up, and we rent a small flat. My pay is low, we've got about three weeks of expenses saved and there are few other electrical employers nearby. I never use AI and prefer the supervisor showing a task with real tools. We talk about stopping work when we can, but I haven't confirmed what retirement income either of us could actually receive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let us learn the job properly without another grand announcement. I'd ask the supervisor to keep showing me the task rather than send me a new screen to guess at. A steady paid shift is useful news to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already anxious about money in this picture. Three weeks saved doesn't cover much time between low wages and rent, and the children being grown up doesn't make our own bills disappear. I like earning, but I don't know how many years of earning our budget still needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised shifts now and through the first year, doing only tasks the qualified supervisor allows and checks. This month I'd cancel the craft magazine renewal, saving thirty over the year for ordinary bills rather than calling it a pension. I'd also ask free household advice how to request our actual retirement-income records and eligibility information, counting no payment until confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even if the trade stays familiar. Being fifty-eight has put retirement into our conversations, not put a retirement wage into our bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown-up children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not put their wages into our plan without asking and receiving an actual offer. They have their own homes and bills; I might ask our daughter to help read a letter if she has time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about a supervised shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finishing a task I've been shown and having the supervisor check it properly. I'd rather ask twice than pretend my years in a clothing workshop make me an experienced electrician.

say: I'd ask for **proper practical learning** rather than another screen a junior is expected to understand alone.
I'd value **steady paid shifts** more than a grand announcement.
think: I'm already **anxious about rent**, with low pay and only three weeks of expenses saved.
Grown children do not remove **our own bills**, and retirement income remains unconfirmed.
do: Keep **supervised shifts**, doing only tasks the qualified supervisor permits and checks.
Cancel the **thirty annual magazine renewal**, using the reduction for bills rather than claiming retirement income.
Ask **free household advice** how to obtain actual retirement-income records and eligibility details, counting no unconfirmed payment.
feel: **Anxious about money**, despite relief at keeping familiar supervised work.
S0.quote: Being fifty-eight has put retirement into our conversations, not put a retirement wage into our bank.
fieldNote: Her **late entry** follows clothing-workshop closure; the vocational certificate does not grant a licence, independent testing or experienced electrical competence.
The **retirement enquiry** seeks actual records and eligibility, with no assumed payment, age entitlement or contribution from grown children.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts only on tasks the qualified supervisor permits and checks
Cancel the thirty annual craft-magazine renewal to help cover bills
Ask free advice how to obtain retirement-income records and eligibility, counting no unconfirmed payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can change its paperwork, but somebody still has to show a beginner the physical task. I'd ask the supervisor what paid hours are actually there, not argue that every new system is wrong. I want to work, not be praised for pressing a button I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid shifts could shrink if the qualified electrician can combine more visits and needs less junior help between jobs. Ben's cleaning is physical, but one wage isn't enough to make our rent easy. There are few local firms, and I'm not ready to offer electrical work on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the employer for the coming month's paid hours in writing and keep a paper note of the tasks I can do under supervision. In the first year I'd keep only permitted supervised work and ask for any compulsory new form to be demonstrated in paid time with my normal weekly wages and hours protected. We'd keep the magazine cancelled while using actual wages, not hoped-for extra shifts, for the rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and embarrassed when I need another explanation. I can be willing to work and still need someone to show me a compulsory work form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer suggests using AI to teach yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a qualified person to show the actual task and check I can do it. I never use AI, and a convincing answer doesn't tell the supervisor whether my hands followed the right steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for your own course to keep the hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without knowing the real task, provider, fees and wage cost. I can't lose the rent money to demonstrate enthusiasm, and I haven't chosen or enrolled in a course.

say: I'd ask for **physical demonstrations** for a beginner even when office paperwork changes.
I'd want **actual paid hours** rather than an argument that every new system is wrong.
think: My **junior shifts could shrink** if faster planning reduces help needed between visits.
Ben's **physical cleaning wage** cannot make the rent easy alone, and few firms offer local alternatives.
do: Request **written monthly hours** now and record tasks I can do under a qualified supervisor.
Keep **permitted supervised work** and require paid personal instruction for compulsory forms, protecting normal weekly wages and hours.
Keep the **magazine cancelled** and budget rent from actual wages rather than possible extra shifts.
feel: **Anxious and embarrassed**, needing instruction without wanting willingness confused with instant understanding.
S1.quote: I can be willing to work and still need someone to show me a compulsory work form.
fieldNote: Her **income risk** comes through junior hours and faster coordination, without claiming thinking software immediately carries out physical electrical tasks.
She keeps **AI non-use** and practical supervision explicit, with no unfunded course commitment or assumption that the other household wage is enough.

steps.text: Keep only permitted supervised work and request written paid hours for the coming month
Require compulsory-form instruction during paid time with normal weekly wages and hours protected
Keep the annual magazine renewal cancelled, budgeting rent from actual wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, and neither date is a retirement agreement for me. I'd ask for the paid supervised tasks the firm actually expects to offer. I'd tell the children we're checking facts, not ask them to promise a missing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when the physical robots follow. I expect a large loss of the simple paid tasks I can do once those robots spread, and Ben's cleaning could change too. With three weeks saved and no confirmed retirement income, I'd be awake wondering what pays the rent between wages and any future entitlement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Ben and I would take actual wages, rent and essential bills to free household advice and request written retirement-income and eligibility records. I'd ask our daughter if she has time to help read the letters, without assuming either her time or money. In 2029 I'd keep only paid supervised tasks actually offered and within my ability, budgeting no retirement payment or extra shift before it is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can make a call if Ben sits beside me. I don't yet know a paid route I can actually afford. I won't pretend my birthday provides a funded route from a lost shift to a paid retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the records show no payment at the age you hoped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd use that answer in the budget instead of the age we'd talked about. I'd ask the adviser what actual options and conditions exist, not simply rename the gap early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask your daughter for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about one evening to read the actual letters, and accept if work or family means she can't. Our daughter's wages aren't money we can put against rent because we're frightened.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** and robots around 2031 from any unconfirmed retirement date.
I'd ask for **paid supervised tasks**, without asking the grown children to promise replacement wages.
think: I expect **large simple-task losses** when robots arrive around age sixty-three, with Ben's physical work also exposed.
Our **three-week reserve** and unconfirmed retirement income leave a rent gap I cannot yet fund.
do: Seek **free household advice** with actual wages, rent and bills, requesting written retirement-income and eligibility records.
Ask our daughter for **letter-reading help** only if she has time, counting no contribution from her wages.
Keep **2029 paid supervised tasks** only where actually offered and within my ability, counting no unconfirmed wage or retirement payment.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, able to seek facts but without a confirmed income bridge.
S2.quote: I won't pretend my birthday provides a funded route from a lost shift to a paid retirement.
fieldNote: She correctly reaches **sixty and sixty-three** at the thinking and physical dates, without assuming age creates a retirement entitlement or affordable exit.
Her **support requests** use actual records and conditional help reading letters, not presumed advice appointments, grown-child payments or continued electrical employment.

steps.text: Ask free advice about actual wages, rent and retirement-income records, counting no unconfirmed payment
Ask our daughter for letter-reading time only if available, not money assumed for rent
Keep paid supervised tasks in 2029 only if offered and within ability

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us get the paperwork about our own income in order before planning changes in 2031. The physical robots follow around 2034, not at the same time. I'd still want the firm to teach a permitted task properly rather than wave a new form at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three at the thinking date and sixty-six when the robots follow. My hours could shrink, but I don't know whether actual retirement income or different paid work will cover our costs by then. More time helps us check, without turning a hoped-for retirement into a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the actual retirement-income records now and review them with Ben and free advice if we can obtain it. We'd check actual wages and essential costs every six months, sooner if a paid shift disappears. In 2032 I'd budget only confirmed wages or retirement income and, if still working, accept only paid tasks my qualified supervisor permits and checks that are within my ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less cornered than in the short picture. I could see the letters and ask another question before somebody tells us a wage has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An actual affordable income plan or work I could no longer do safely might make me stop. I'd ask about the real options before calling an exit possible. I haven't chosen early retirement just because I've circled a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in training while waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a real practical task, a place, fees paid and no lost weekly wages before choosing. For now I'm asking about records and keeping permitted paid work, not buying a qualification on hope.

say: I'd use **five years** to obtain income records before thinking AI in 2031 and later physical robots.
I'd keep asking for **proper task instruction**, not treat a form as practical teaching.
think: My **hours could shrink** before we know what confirmed income meets costs at sixty-three or sixty-six.
More time supports **checking records**, not a promise of affordable retirement or another paid role.
do: Request **retirement-income records** now and review them with Ben, seeking free advice if available.
Check **actual wages and essentials** every six months, sooner if shifts fall.
Budget only confirmed income in 2032; if working, keep **supervised tasks** only when permitted, checked and within ability.
feel: **Anxious but less cornered**, with more time to read actual records before deciding anything.
S3.quote: I haven't chosen early retirement just because I've circled a birthday.
fieldNote: She correctly reaches **sixty-three and sixty-six**, and allows retirement or different work only as possibilities requiring actual affordability and safe tasks.
Her **course enquiry** does not become enrolment, and any later electrical work remains conditional on availability, ability and qualified supervision.

steps.text: Request retirement records; seek available free advice and review costs with Ben every six months
Budget only confirmed wages or retirement income in 2032
Take offered paid tasks only within ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is room to make one checked decision at a time, not a promise I'll still be climbing about in houses. I'd keep asking what income actually exists and what work I can safely do. The grown children need honest answers, not a duty to fund a plan we haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when physical robots follow around 2039. I might already have stopped work or still need earnings; I can't say until we have real figures. Today's low pay and short reserve still make me anxious, even when those dates are farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the same actual income and eligibility records now and review essential costs with Ben every six months. In 2037 we'd use only confirmed wages, support or retirement income in the budget, seeking free advice if actual income misses essentials and an appointment is available. If I'm still doing electrical work then, it must be offered, paid, within my ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor; none of those is guaranteed by this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present rent, but less rushed by a distant machine date. I can talk about a possible quieter life without announcing that somebody has agreed to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you write your children's future help into the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask about any actual offer rather than turn family affection into a monthly payment. They may have their own difficulties by then, and I don't know their future money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep doing while the records are unclear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current supervised paid shifts while offered and safe, and ask the employer for the actual hours. I wouldn't claim the same job will be there at sixty-eight simply because I need the money.

I'd ask for actual income and **safe tasks**, without treating grown children as an unchecked funding plan.
think: At **sixty-eight and seventy-one**, I cannot assume either retirement income or continuing electrical employment.
Our low pay and **short reserve** still make today's rent worrying despite the longer warning.
do: Request **actual income records** now and review essential costs with Ben every six months.
Use only **confirmed income** in 2037 and seek free advice if essentials fail and an appointment is available.
Keep electrical work only when **offered and paid**, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor.
feel: **Anxious about present rent**, with more time to ask about a quieter life without assuming it is funded.
S4.quote: I wouldn't claim the same job will be there at sixty-eight simply because I need the money.
fieldNote: Her **older ages** remain explicit, without assuming a job at sixty-eight, pension date, amount or entitlement to calm the picture.
The **budget conditions** require confirmed income and available advice, while family help and any future supervised work remain uncertain rather than guaranteed.

steps.text: Request actual income records now and review essential costs with my partner every six months
Seek free advice in 2037 if confirmed income misses essentials and an appointment is available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect the simple physical tasks I earn from to shrink around 2031 before we know a funded next step. Actual paid hours, patient supervised teaching and free advice using our real income records would help. I'd rather know a disappointing figure than plan rent around a retirement payment nobody has confirmed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the older beginner what she still needs to be shown, not just when she expects to stop. I've worked for years, but not for years as an electrician. My working years don't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.

headlineQuote: My working years don't turn my vocational certificate into an electrician's licence.
portrait: Sara is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning under qualified supervision after a clothing workshop closed.
She has **three weeks saved**, low pay and few nearby firms; partner Ben works cleaning shifts, and their children are grown.
She **never uses AI**, needs repeated practical demonstrations and does only tasks a qualified supervisor permits and checks.
Retirement is **in her thoughts**, but neither age nor family affection supplies a confirmed income bridge or safe future job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected simple-task losses around 2031 before she knows an affordable, funded next step.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual paid hours**, patient supervision and available free advice using real income records would help.
